etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: Circa 1230, Middle English descorde, discorde; from Anglo-Norman, Old French descort (derivative of descorder), descorde (“disagreement”); from Latin discordia, from discors (“disagreeing, disagreement”), from dis- (“apart”) + cor, cordis (“heart”).
Verb derives from Middle English discorden, from Anglo-Norman, Old French descorder, from Latin discordāre, from discord-, as above.
senses: Lack of concord, agreement, harmony; disaccord.
Tension or strife resulting from a lack of agreement; dissension.
(intransitive, archaic) To disagree; to fail to agree or harmonize; clash.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
senses: (transitive, rare) To untie things which are connected by a cord.
